---
title: "Discriminant Analysis"
---

Discriminant analysis is a probability-based approach to
classification. Instead of modeling $\Pr(Y=1 \mid X)$ directly, it
models the distribution of predictors within each class and combines
those distributions with class priors.

## Learning Objectives

- Explain Bayes' rule for classification.
- Distinguish LDA from QDA.
- Interpret class priors, posterior probabilities, and decision
  boundaries.
- Compare logistic regression, LDA, and QDA.
- Evaluate discriminant models with thresholds and ROC-style thinking.

## Bayes' Rule for Classification

For class $k$,

$$
\Pr(Y=k \mid X=x)
= \frac{\pi_k f_k(x)}
{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\pi_\ell f_\ell(x)},
$$

where $\pi_k$ is the prior probability of class $k$ and $f_k(x)$ is the
class-conditional density.

LDA assumes all classes share a covariance matrix. QDA allows each
class to have its own covariance matrix.

## LDA and QDA Example

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| fig-align: center
library(MASS)

set.seed(571)
n <- 400
disc <- data.frame(
  balance = rnorm(n, 1200, 450),
  income = rnorm(n, 60000, 18000)
)
eta <- -5 + 0.003 * disc$balance - 0.00001 * disc$income
disc$default <- factor(rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta)),
                       labels = c("No", "Yes"))

lda_fit <- lda(default ~ balance + income, data = disc)
qda_fit <- qda(default ~ balance + income, data = disc)

lda_prob <- predict(lda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
qda_prob <- predict(qda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
head(lda_prob)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 400
disc = pd.DataFrame({
    "balance": rng.normal(1200, 450, n),
    "income": rng.normal(60000, 18000, n)
})
eta = -5 + 0.003 * disc["balance"] - 0.00001 * disc["income"]
disc["default"] = np.where(rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta))), "Yes", "No")

X = disc[["balance", "income"]]
y = disc["default"]
lda_fit = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)
qda_fit = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)

lda_prob = lda_fit.predict_proba(X)[:, list(lda_fit.classes_).index("Yes")]
qda_prob = qda_fit.predict_proba(X)[:, list(qda_fit.classes_).index("Yes")]
print(lda_prob[:5])
```

:::

LDA is more restrictive but often more stable. QDA is more flexible but
requires more data because it estimates separate covariance structures.

## Comparing with Logistic Regression

Logistic regression and LDA can produce similar boundaries when class
conditional distributions are close to normal with common covariance.
QDA can bend the boundary when covariance differs across classes.
